title: Beijing bolsters South China Sea push with new island runway – analysts
summary: TOKYO, Japan — China is building a runway on another island in the disputed South China Sea that could significantly strengthen its military footprint in the strategic waterway, according to experts…

blocks.text: TOKYO, Japan — China is building a runway on another island in the disputed South China Sea that could significantly strengthen its military footprint in the strategic waterway, according to experts and satellite images seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP).

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea, despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and confrontations have occurred regularly with several Southeast Asian nations over control of the Paracel and Spratly Islands.
Both island chains are essentially made up of reefs and outcrops, but analysts say China has been steadily reclaiming land and building infrastructure to gain military control of the sea.

Beijing late last year began large-scale dredging and reclaiming land at Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands, which are claimed by China, Vietnam and Taiwan, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Lowy Institute said in recent detailed reports, citing satellite images.
Important outpost
Lowell Bautista, author of the Lowy Institute report, told AFP that China transformed the reef in 10 months from one of its smallest Paracel outposts into an island that can rival its largest atoll.

The nearly 3-kilometer runway on Antelope Reef would be Beijing’s second in the Paracels and—together with infrastructure on the Spratly Islands and on Hainan Island—helps “create an integrated network of runways, harbors and sensors stretching across the sea,” Bautista said.
China and Vietnam fought a brief but bloody skirmish over the Paracels in 1974. More than 70 Vietnamese soldiers were killed and China has had de facto control over the islands since then.
The runway is a similar size to an airstrip on the Paracels’ Woody Island and three others across the Spratlys, according to CSIS.
Civilian purposes

Analysts say Antelope—which is around 6 kilometers along its northwest-southeast axis—could become one of China’s most important outposts in the South China Sea, potentially helping Beijing limit the access of US and allied naval forces in the event of conflict.
China says the development of the Paracel Islands, which it adds have a small resident population of mostly fishers, is for civilian purposes.
‘Full control’ of sea

A spokesperson for the foreign ministry said in March that China’s land reclamation activities there are “necessary construction” for “improving living and working conditions on the islands and growing the local economy.”
A structure that appears to be a runway is clearly visible in photos taken in September by Earth imaging company Planet Labs.
The images were reviewed as part of a recent report by Japanese intelligence firm Deep Dive and were also seen by AFP.

Deep Dive director Bonji Ohara, a former defense attaché in China, said in the report that the structure would be able to handle not just fighter jets but also larger aircraft, including transport planes, aerial refueling tankers and bombers.
The new runway could potentially bring China closer to achieving “full control over the entire South China Sea,” he said.

CSIS has said that Antelope could enhance the reach of Chinese sensing capabilities closer to Vietnam’s shores and help expand its military capacity in an area of the northern South China Sea which is close to major shipping lanes.
Antelope Reef’s runway is expected to be operational by mid-2027, although other analysts were more cautious about its significance.

The runway and harbor will “add additional capacity and resilience to the facility that enable China’s military and paramilitary operations in the South China Sea,” Harrison Pretat, deputy director at CSIS’s Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, told AFP.
Limited pushback
But “Southeast Asian claimants have still largely maintained access to offshore resources and occupy their own outposts,” he said.

Nevertheless, Pretat warned that “international attention and pushback … has been far less than might be expected given the scale and significance” of construction, due in part “to distraction from other global crises.”

“Regional countries … along with the United States and the international community, should be speaking with a stronger voice against island building and other attempts to permanently alter conditions in disputed areas,” he said.
‘Completely illegal’
Vietnam in August called construction at Antelope Reef “completely illegal” and demanded “such activities cease immediately.”

And in October, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said that China’s military buildup was creating a “condition of pressure” in Southeast Asia, and urged allies and partners to deepen cooperation.

But Hunter Marston of the Lowy Institute told AFP that “Asean (Association of Southeast Asian Nations member-states) will never be capable of communicating with one voice” due partly to their different views of China.

US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the sea, and Filipino and Chinese ships have engaged in repeated confrontations in recent years, some leading to collisions and injuries.
Ohara said that Beijing views the sea as “a sanctuary … where it does not want foreign powers to enter in the event of a contingency” in the region.

“While it will not restrict freedom of navigation in peacetime, if some incident occurs, China intends to prevent not only US naval forces but also those of its allies—for example, Australian submarines—from entering,” he said. /cb
